title: Shipped a complete Godot 4.6 mobile game through an AI pipeline in 160 hours: code, art, audio, balance and text in 10 languages were all generated. Pipeline and failure modes inside.
author: mrMaygreen
selftext:
This is a write-up of an experiment: can an AI pipeline carry a game all the way to a store release, not a prototype or a jam entry. The answer is yes with caveats, and the caveats are the useful part. The Last War: Train Defense is out on Google Play (Android). Total effort from idea to release: 160 hours.

**Who did what**

The GDScript, the art, the sound effects and music, the balance passes, the text and the localization into 10 languages were generated. The commits in the repository were made by agents, the verification tooling included. My part was to set the task, build the pipelines and tooling the agents worked in, specify the gates they had to pass, review and sign off the results, and test the builds on a real phone. The point of the experiment was the tooling rather than the game: how much verification has to sit around generation before the output can be trusted enough to ship. There is no generative AI inside the game; everything was produced before release.

**The pipeline, in one paragraph**

Code: LLM coding agents working in a Godot 4.6 repo, with a project-level instruction file, a headless parse check, a boot smoke that runs the real app for a few hundred frames, and a combat smoke that jumps straight into a fight. Art: diffusion models through Leonardo.ai and a local ComfyUI on one RTX 4090, background removal by ML segmentation. Audio: Stable Audio Open, run locally. Balance: simulator runs of missions rather than hand-tuning. Text: key-based .po files across 10 locales with extraction and apply tooling.

**Where it broke**

- It wrote a bug that would have wiped the player's save on boot. The code read fine. Neither review nor the smoke tests caught it; a dedicated audit did. Plausible-looking wrong code is the main failure mode of the whole approach, and it is exactly the kind that gets past a skim. Anything touching the save schema now gets a load round-trip check as a rule.
- The audio model cannot do short transients. Explosions and music came out usable; anything under about 0.3 s turned to mush. Several UI ticks stayed procedural, and the gunshot is a hybrid: a generated boom layer under a synthesized band-noise crack, because neither alone read as a gun.
- Image-to-video was tried for the trailer and rejected outright. It did not match the game's art direction, and a trailer that looks like a different game is worse than no trailer. The video linked below is a straight engine capture through Godot Movie Maker.
- Background agents die and take their work with them. Long unattended jobs got killed mid-flight often enough that anything expensive now runs in the foreground. A stray git checkout also wiped uncommitted localization work once; the reconstructed lines needed a human read-through, because nobody could tell which ones had been silently rewritten.
- Chroma-key background removal ate the artwork. Flood fill cannot tell dark gunmetal on the subject from a dark background. ML segmentation fixed it.
- The warm-cache parse gate was lying. Godot's `--headless --editor --quit` with a warm `.godot` cache hides dangling `class_name` references, so a cascade of "class not found" errors pointed at a live class while the real culprit was a different file failing to compile. Now there is a cold-cache scan and a linter for dangling class references.
- The dumbest perf bug: per-item `print()` in the boot path cost over a second of startup on Windows. Grep for `print(` before profiling anything cleverer.

**What I would tell someone starting the same experiment**

Generation was never the bottleneck. Trusting the output was. Most of the human effort went into the gates: deciding what runs before a commit is accepted, what runs on a real phone, and what gets audited on principle regardless of how clean it looks. Skip that part and you get a repository full of confident code that nobody has checked.

**The game itself, for context**

Dieselpunk arcade AA-survival, portrait, one finger. An armored train holds station while enemies dive from above. The AA turrets fire on their own and you never aim; your finger drags a harvest field to catch falling crystals and triggers reactor abilities. Every level-up gives three cards to choose from with no skip, around thirteen of those decisions per mission. Nine guns with five levels each; at level three a gun forks into one of three paths (27 across the nine), and gun pairs link automatically when both are mounted. Ten biomes of ten missions each, 100 in all, with a phased boss closing every biome and a mini-boss in the other missions; you can start from any unlocked biome. Between runs, crystals go into an upgrade tree, alongside four locomotives, wagons carrying reactor abilities, modules in six roles and four rarities, research, reward crates and a bestiary. Runs are free, no energy or timers; single-player, plays offline; a mission takes several minutes. Optional IAP, ads are rewarded-only. Holds 30 FPS on a Helio G85.

Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=net.didogames.thelastwar
Presentation video (70 s, engine capture): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iQkJA8OJrKU
Press kit, with the full list of what was and was not generated: https://didogames.net/en/press.html
Site: https://didogames.net/en/

Happy to answer questions on the pipeline, the verification harness, the model choices, or any of the failures above.

comments.author: Game_and_data
comments.body: What did you use to orchestrate everything? Cursor, something else ? Thanks for sharing, but the post try to tell everything at once and without your context is really hard to read and understand.

replies.author: mrMaygreen
replies.body: Claude Code, run as agents against the repo: a project instruction file at the root, plus a set of role agents (producer, tutorial developer, art director, QA, publishing) that hand work to each other and have to pass the same gates before anything is accepted. Art went through Leonardo's API and a local ComfyUI, audio through Stable Audio Open on a local card. Fair point on the density of the post; the full breakdown of what was and was not generated is on the press kit page, and I will answer anything specific here.

replies.author: mrMaygreen
replies.body: Thanks for actually installing it, that is worth more to me than the rest of the thread. You hit a real bug: the tutorial log fades out 4.5 seconds after it stops typing, no matter how long the line is, so the longer hints vanish before anyone can read them. The fix is going in now: the delay scales with the length of the text, and lines that ask you to do something stay until you act.

replies.author: mrMaygreen
replies.body: Fair suspicion, and most of what ships under this banner earns it. On the steps you list, for the record: the first core loop was thrown out and rebuilt because it was not fun; the build ran a closed test on Google Play with outside testers before release; and the last three weeks were bug fixes and balance passes from that test, plus the tutorial fix from the comment above. Whether that adds up to a game worth your time is your call. The write-up is about where the pipeline failed, not a pitch, and the trailer is engine capture, so what you see on the store page is what runs.

comments.author: mrMaygreen
comments.body: Correct. The post was drafted by the same pipeline, then edited and signed off by me, the same way as everything else in the project. That is the experiment; pretending otherwise would be worse than saying so.

comments.author: BugCatcherBacardi
comments.body: Your use of Claude is load bearing and there’s 3 key signs, one significant that deserves your attention: even your replies to comments are AI generated slop, a serious footgun that impacts the seam of where your game intersects with desirability.

replies.author: mrMaygreen
replies.body: As I wrote earlier, this is an experiment; the game doesn't aim to be commercially successful. And my experiment showed that creating a truly compelling project solely based on artificial intelligence is currently impossible. For now, very close human participation is necessary.

comments.author: RocketSciense
comments.body: Real question OP. Your post and all of your responses are clearly AI generated.  The tone, language, everything about it.  It's one thing to share the game but to not even write here on reddit is another thing.  We do NOT want to be interacting with bots on reddit. What drives you to do this?

replies.author: mrMaygreen
replies.body: I answer the questions myself, simply translating them using AI, and also adapting the text. This is the essence of my experiment: what level have current capabilities reached and what are the limitations? I understand that everyone is very wary of using artificial intelligence these days, but this is part of my experiment.

comments.author: mrMaygreen
comments.body: Before writing a comment, make sure that your opinion is really needed.

comments.author: mrMaygreen
comments.body: I understand that you are unhappy with artificial intelligence, but what are you doing in a group where artificial intelligence is discussed?

comments.author: mrMaygreen
comments.body: I don't give advice, and I don't think it's worth throwing around advice. I conducted an experiment and shared the results. I don't give advice, and I don't need advice. So, you can keep your advice to yourself and continue doing your own thing instead of engaging with Claude in the comments.
